extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal researchers, and anyone researching federal administrative agencies and regulations
extracted.subtask_description: A practical research guide to finding and updating federal regulations, rulemaking materials, agency decisions, and executive/regulatory history for work involving federal administrative agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA rulemaking procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) agencies must: Publish a notice of proposed rulemaking in the Federal Register; Take comments from 'interested persons' on the proposed rule; Publish a final rule in the Federal Register after considering those comments; Make the rule effective not less than 30 days after it is published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APA contains the key procedural steps agencies must follow when putting rules into effect; follow these steps when researching the lifecycle of a regulation and when assessing whether procedure required by law was observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA grounds for judicial review (5 U.S.C. § 706)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are instructed to set aside agency actions that are 'arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law'; 'contrary to constitutional right, power, privilege, or immunity'; 'in excess of statutory jurisdiction, authority, or limitations, or short of statutory right'; or 'without observance of procedure required by law.' (5 U.S.C. § 706).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these statutory standards when evaluating the legal vulnerability of regulations and when searching for cases or commentary challenging agency action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Register contents and what to look for
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rules and NPRMs include not just the regulatory text but also: a summary of the rule; the rule's effective date; a detailed description of the rule's history, context, and purpose; a section-by-section analysis; responses to public comments (for final rules); and explanations of specific amendments or changes from proposed to final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When doing regulatory history research, consult the Federal Register to find explanation, justification, and the agency's responses to comments — materials often critical to interpretation and to administrative-law challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Federal Register and related access points
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Register is available via FederalRegister.gov (1994- ), GovInfo.gov (1936- ), HeinOnline, Westlaw, and LexisNexis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FederalRegister.gov has excellent navigation and search tools but only back to 1994; GovInfo provides PDFs of every issue; HeinOnline, Westlaw, and Lexis provide subscription access. Choose the source appropriate to your coverage needs and access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The CFR contains general and permanent rules organized into 50 topical titles, with chapters (typically a single agency), parts, subparts, and sections. Citations typically appear at the part or section level (e.g., 21 C.F.R. § 101.22).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the title/part/section structure to locate rules and to cite them properly; consult subject indexes and eCFR agency indexes when searching by topic or agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: CFR source notes are valuable for regulatory history
rubrics_metrics.description: A Source Note at the beginning of each CFR part provides the citation to where the Final Rule creating or amending the part was published in the Federal Register; if a section was added or amended later, a separate source note appears at the end of that section's text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Source Notes to trace the Federal Register publication(s) that created or amended CFR text; the Final Rule often contains explanatory materials useful for history and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: CFR updates and the difference between CFR and Federal Register
rubrics_metrics.description: The CFR incorporates amendments published in the Federal Register with each update; the official print CFR is updated in stages quarterly (Titles 1–16: Jan 1; 17–27: Apr 1; 28–41: July 1; 42–50: Oct 1). The Federal Register contains the daily publication of proposed and final rules and supporting materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the CFR is updated only periodically, always check for recent Federal Register notices or consult eCFR and other tools to ensure regulatory language is current.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check currency with citators and update tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Use citators (Shepard's, KeyCite) to check cases citing the rule for adverse treatment and to identify proposed or finalized amendments; citators may flag regulations with proposed amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citators are often the fastest way to find adverse judicial treatment or pending amendments; follow citator flags with primary-source checks in the Federal Register or eCFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update research using eCFR, FederalRegister.gov, and LSA
rubrics_metrics.description: Free online sources to update regulations include eCFR.gov, FederalRegister.gov, and the List of Sections Affected (LSA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use eCFR for current (unofficial) codified text, FederalRegister.gov for recent rulemaking documents, and the LSA to identify CFR sections affected by final rules since the last official CFR update.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using FederalRegister.gov Advanced Document Search to find changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Search > Advanced Document Search, use the field 'Affecting CFR Part' and enter the relevant part number to find updates or proposed changes affecting a CFR part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This search field is a targeted way to locate Federal Register documents that claim to affect a particular CFR part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stepwise use of the List of Sections Affected (LSA)
rubrics_metrics.description: To update with the LSA: Find the regulation text in the CFR and note the revision date; check the most recent LSA and compare coverage dates; if there's a gap, check annual cumulations of the LSA; check the 'CFR Parts Affected during [month]' list in Federal Register issues for months not covered; check the cumulative list in the last issue for the current month; use citations found to read relevant Federal Register issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The LSA helps you identify specific Federal Register issues affecting CFR sections when the printed CFR volume is out of date; follow the listed steps to ensure you capture intervening changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory history research sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory history useful materials are in the Federal Register; docket materials and public comments are on Regulations.gov; compiled rulemaking materials for a Public Law or Executive Order may be in ProQuest Regulatory Insight; Library of Congress provides a 'How to Trace Federal Regulations' guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine Federal Register narrative materials with docket materials on Regulations.gov and secondary compilations to reconstruct why and how a rule was made and changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start at the agency website for agency-specific materials
rubrics_metrics.description: If working with a specific agency, the agency's website is a great place to start; look for sections titled 'Rules & Regulations', 'Legal / Laws Library', 'Enforcement', 'Interpretations'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many agencies post rules, guidance, enforcement decisions, and advisory materials on their own websites; agency sites can also link to dockets and archived decisions not centrally published.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency decisions: where to find adjudicative or interpretive decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies issue decisions in a judicial-like capacity; these are rarely gathered in one place and some agencies do not publish decisions. Useful starting points include agency websites and secondary resource links like the University of Virginia Law Library's Administrative Decisions Website Links.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial databases (Westlaw Administrative Decisions & Guidance, LexisNexis Administrative Law Decisions, VitalLaw) may collect decisions; some agencies publish official reporters or loose-leaf services—check Bluebook tables T1.2 and T15 and library catalogs (e.g., Hollis) for print holdings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) for agency documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Under FOIA, you may request documents from administrative agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When records or docket materials are not publicly posted, consider FOIA requests; consult guides to FOIA procedures and exemptions when planning requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive materials and OIRA oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive materials (Executive Orders, Presidential Documents) are found in Title 3 of the CFR and in the Presidential Documents section of the Federal Register. OIRA (within OMB) reviews federal regulations, publishes the Unified Agenda and Regulatory Plan, and posts current and past regulatory reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult Title 3, the White House, OIRA pages, the Unified Agenda, and Presidential Documents when the regulatory action involves or was influenced by executive-level decisions or OIRA review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use secondary sources and current-awareness tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary sources — books, news/current-awareness sources, scholarly articles, advocacy communications, law reviews, and 'blawgs' — are helpful starting points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Westlaw/Lexis secondary materials, administrative law journals, ABA and other blawgs to get context, commentary, and citations pointing to primary materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation form for CFR and Bluebook guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: CFR citations are governed by Bluebook Rule 14. Example: 17 C.F.R. § 275.250 (2011).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Bluebook conventions when citing regulations in legal writing; cite at the part or section level as appropriate and include year parenthetical where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Library and librarian resources for assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Contact librarians via email, chat, or schedule an online consult; use library catalogs for print materials (Hollis) and special collections contact points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When research tasks are complex (regulatory history, archival decisions, FOIA), consult law librarians or schedule consultations to identify resources and search strategies efficiently.
